name: MA 162 — Exam 3 (Lessons 21–27)
description: Decision-first: which test, what setup, what trap. Sequences, series tests, power & Taylor series, polar.

cards.front: What's the difference between a sequence converging and a series converging?
cards.back: A sequence is a list a₁, a₂, …; a series is the SUM of those terms. Converging sequence: terms settle down. Converging series: partial sums settle down. Different objects, different tests.

cards.front: lim_{n→∞} (ln n)/n: how do you evaluate a limit with n in it?
cards.back: 1. Treat a_n as f(n) for a continuous f, use L'Hôpital on f(x), then transfer the limit back. Trap: you may only L'Hôpital the continuous version, never the raw sequence.

cards.front: a_n = (−1)ⁿ: converges or diverges?
cards.back: Diverges — it oscillates between −1 and 1 forever. A limit must settle on ONE number.

cards.front: Σ_{n=1}^∞ (5/7)ⁿ: geometric? First term, ratio, sum?
cards.back: r = 5/7, first term a = 5/7 (n starts at 1). Sum = a/(1−r) = (5/7)/(2/7) = 5/2. Trap: a is the FIRST term of the sum, not the coefficient pattern.

cards.front: Geometric series Σ arⁿ converges if and only if what? What breaks at r = 1?
cards.back: |r| < 1. At r = 1 the terms don't shrink (sum explodes); at r = −1 they oscillate. The formula a/(1−r) only applies when |r| < 1.

cards.front: Σ n/(2n+1): converges or diverges? Which test kills it in one line?
cards.back: It diverges by the divergence test: lim a_n = 1/2 ≠ 0. Any series whose terms don't tend to 0 is dead on arrival.

cards.front: lim a_n = 0. Does Σ a_n converge?
cards.back: Inconclusive — it tells you NOTHING. lim a_n = 0 is necessary but not sufficient for series convergence (harmonic series: terms → 0, sum diverges).

cards.front: What two properties guarantee a sequence converges?
cards.back: Bounded AND monotone ⟹ converges (Monotone Convergence Theorem). Bounded alone isn't enough — (−1)ⁿ is bounded but diverges.

cards.front: Σ 1/n³: which test, and verdict?
cards.back: p-series with p = 3 > 1: converges. (Same p > 1 rule as the p-integral — one rule, two settings.)

cards.front: Σ 1/√n: converges or diverges?
cards.back: p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1: diverges. Trap: it LOOKS like the terms shrink fast enough. They don't.

cards.front: Σ n!/10ⁿ: which test? Verdict?
cards.back: Factorials ⟹ ratio test. L = lim (n+1)!/10ⁿ⁺¹ · 10ⁿ/n! = lim (n+1)/10 = ∞ > 1: diverges.

cards.front: Σ (2n/(3n+1))ⁿ: which test? Verdict?
cards.back: Root test — the (…)^n form is its signature. L = lim 2n/(3n+1) = 2/3 < 1: converges.

cards.front: Σ (−1)ⁿ/√n: which test? Absolute or conditional?
cards.back: Alternating series test: b_n = 1/√n decreasing → 0, so it converges. Since Σ 1/√n diverges, convergence is CONDITIONAL.

cards.front: Ratio test gives L = 1. What do you conclude?
cards.back: Nothing — L = 1 is INCONCLUSIVE. Classic trap: Σ 1/n and Σ 1/n² both give L = 1, but one diverges and one converges. Fall back to comparison.

cards.front: Σ 1/(n²+5n): what do you compare against, and verdict?
cards.back: Limit comparison with b_n = 1/n² (the dominant term): ratio → 1, and Σ 1/n² converges, so Σ 1/(n²+5n) converges.

cards.front: Σ_{n=2}^∞ 1/(n ln n): which test? Verdict?
cards.back: Integral test: ∫₂^∞ dx/(x ln x) = lim ln(ln t) = ∞, diverges. The ln in the denominator is the integral test's signature move.

cards.front: You approximated an alternating series with N terms. Bound the error.
cards.back: |error| ≤ b_{N+1}, the first OMITTED term. Only valid for alternating series satisfying the AST conditions.

cards.front: §10.9 decision tree: match each series shape to its test.
cards.back: Factorials and exponentials → ratio; (…)^n forms → root; alternating → AST; rational functions → comparison/limit comparison; 1/(n·(ln n)^p) → integral.

cards.front: Σ xⁿ/n!: radius of convergence?
cards.back: R = ∞ — it converges for every x. Signature: factorials in the DENOMINATOR crush any fixed xⁿ.

cards.front: Σ n!xⁿ: radius of convergence?
cards.back: R = 0 — converges only at x = 0. Signature: factorials in the NUMERATOR crush everything.

cards.front: Σ xⁿ/n: full interval of convergence?
cards.back: Ratio test gives R = 1. x = 1: Σ 1/n diverges (harmonic) — reject. x = −1: Σ (−1)ⁿ/n converges (AST) — keep. Interval: [−1, 1).

cards.front: Differentiate Σ xⁿ/n term by term. New radius?
cards.back: Same radius R = 1 — differentiation never changes the radius. Endpoints can change, so recheck them.

cards.front: Maclaurin series for 1/(1−x)? On what interval?
cards.back: Σ xⁿ for |x| < 1 — it's the geometric series with a = 1, r = x. Everything about power series starts here.

cards.front: Get the Maclaurin series for e^{2x} from the eˣ series.
cards.back: Σ (2x)ⁿ/n! = Σ 2ⁿxⁿ/n!. Substituting into a known series is legal — you inherit its radius (R = ∞ here).

cards.front: Maclaurin series for x·e^{x²}?
cards.back: x·Σ x^{2n}/n! = Σ x^{2n+1}/n!. Multiply series termwise; radius stays ∞.

cards.front: lim_{x→0} (sin x − x)/x³ via series?
cards.back: sin x = x − x³/6 + ⋯, so (sin x − x)/x³ = −1/6 + x²/120 − ⋯ → −1/6. Series turn 0/0 limits into reading the first surviving term.

cards.front: Maclaurin polynomial P₂(x) for eˣ?
cards.back: 1 + x + x²/2. Coefficients are f^{(k)}(0)/k!: 1, 1, 1/2.

cards.front: Maclaurin polynomial P₃(x) for sin x?
cards.back: x − x³/6. Odd function ⟹ only odd powers; coefficients 1, −1/6 from 1/1!, −1/3!.

cards.front: General coefficient of (x−a)ⁿ in a Taylor polynomial?
cards.back: f^{(n)}(a)/n!. The factorial undoes the n! that the power rule spits out when differentiating xⁿ — that's the whole reason it's there.

cards.front: You need to approximate f(1.1). Where do you center the Taylor polynomial?
cards.back: Center at a = 1 (or wherever you're approximating). Taylor error grows with |x − a|, so center near your target — not always at 0.

cards.front: Lagrange form of the remainder? How do you turn it into a usable error bound?
cards.back: R_n = f^{(n+1)}(c)/(n+1)! · (x−a)^{n+1} for some c between a and x. Bound it by replacing |f^{(n+1)}(c)| with its max on the interval.

cards.front: Why is using a Maclaurin polynomial to estimate e¹⁰ a bad idea?
cards.back: Maclaurin series are centered at 0, so at x = 10 the error term (10^{n+1}/(n+1)!) is enormous unless n is huge. Center near your target instead.

cards.front: Polar point (2, π/3): rectangular coordinates?
cards.back: (1, √3). x = 2·cos(π/3) = 1, y = 2·sin(π/3) = √3. Formulas: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.

cards.front: x² + y² = 9 in polar form?
cards.back: r = 3. Replace: x² + y² = r², so r² = 9 ⟹ r = 3. Circles centered at the origin are trivial in polar.

cards.front: r = 2 cos θ: what shape?
cards.back: A circle through the origin, diameter 2 along the x-axis (center (1,0), radius 1). r = a cos θ ⟹ circle on the x-axis.

cards.front: r = 3 cos(2θ): how many petals?
cards.back: 4 petals. r = a cos(nθ): n petals if n is odd, 2n petals if n is even. Here n = 2 (even) ⟹ 4.

cards.front: Area formula in polar? What's the most-forgotten piece?
cards.back: A = ∫ (1/2)r² dθ. The 1/2 is the #1 forgotten factor — it comes from the sector area formula (1/2)r²θ.

cards.front: Give another polar name for (3, π/6) with a negative r.
cards.back: (−3, 7π/6): flip r's sign and add π to θ. Same point, infinitely many names — (r,θ) = (−r, θ+π).

cards.front: Arc length formula in polar?
cards.back: L = ∫ √(r² + (dr/dθ)²) dθ. It's the √(1+(y′)²) idea rewritten for polar — the (dr/dθ)² term accounts for radial stretching.

cards.front: r = 1 + cos θ vs r = 2 + cos θ: which is the cardioid, and why?
cards.back: r = 1 + cos θ is a cardioid; r = 2 + cos θ (bigger constant) is a dimpled limacon; r = 0.5 + cos θ is an inner-loop limacon. The a/b ratio decides.
